captions.gbp:
November is diabetes awareness month, and a good time to ask your doctor about your bones. According to the NIH's Diabetes in America, people with type 2 diabetes have about a 70% higher risk of hip fracture, even when their bone density is average or higher, and type 1 diabetes raises hip fracture risk too. Falls play a part, so fall prevention, staying active and good nutrition all help. Questions worth asking at your next visit: Does my diabetes raise my fracture risk? Should I have a bone density (DEXA) scan, and how often? Could any of my medicines affect my bones? What can I do to lower my risk of falls? Screening guidelines differ: the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for women 65 and older and younger women after menopause with risk factors, and finds the evidence insufficient for men, so decide with your doctor. Advanced Medical Imaging in Seminole offers DEXA bone density scans for $75 self-pay, radiologist reading included. The scan takes about 10 minutes, fully clothed, and results go to your doctor in 48 to 72 hours. With insurance, a doctor's order is needed. Using Medicare? Ask us what applies.

Book online at advancedimg.com. General information, not medical advice.

facts_checked: 2026-11-06: NIH/NIDDK Diabetes in America 3rd ed., ch. 32 Bone and Joint Complications in Diabetes (Schwartz & Lane; abstract: type 2 diabetes, in spite of average or higher BMD, hip fracture risk up about 70%, non-spine about 20%; type 1 about sevenfold hip fracture risk; more frequent falls contribute; prevention via falls reduction, physical activity, nutrition; BMD-based methods tend to underestimate risk in T2D). USPSTF osteoporosis screening final 2025 (women 65+; postmenopausal <65 at increased risk; men insufficient). amiweb 695772f: prices.ts dexa $75 Seminole; services-data.ts dexa (about 10 min fully clothed, results 48-72 h, self-pay no referral, insurance needs order).
flag: Hook and Google photo service-dexa.jpg is a website stock image (not AMI staff or patient). Diabetes source is NIH's Diabetes in America chapter (finalized 2016), the most authoritative US summary found; 'American Diabetes Month' is an ADA trademark, so the post says 'diabetes awareness month'. Many readers will be on Medicare: post says 'ask us what applies'. Website DEXA FAQ says 'women 65+ and men 70+ should get a baseline DEXA'; USPSTF 2025 finds evidence insufficient for men (Endocrine/BHOF advise 70+), so the website wording may need a 'guidelines differ' note. Facebook link uses /schedule (the DEXA landing page is body-composition focused).
